analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid painkiller makers to fund state addiction treatment programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: a one-cent-per-milligram tax on opioid manufacturers to fund addiction treatment died with zero cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged opioid manufacturers one cent per milligram on the painkillers they sell. The money raised, after rebates, would flow to states to pay for addiction treatment — new clinics, residential programs, recovery housing, and care for babies born dependent on opioids. Cancer and hospice patients would be rebated so they never pay the tax, and addiction-treatment drugs like methadone and buprenorphine would be exempt entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction and their families, who would gain state-funded treatment options: new residential and outpatient facilities, sober living homes, long-term 30/60/90-day programs, job and housing support for people in recovery, and care for infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome. States would receive dedicated funding for these programs. Cancer and hospice patients are protected through rebates or point-of-sale discounts so they bear none of the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Directs every dollar of net tax revenue to states for substance abuse treatment — new treatment facilities, sober living homes, long-term residential programs, recovery housing and job support, and facilities for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome.
Exempts drugs used exclusively for medication-assisted treatment of opioid addiction, so the tax would not raise the price of medicines like methadone or buprenorphine that treat addiction itself.
Shields cancer and hospice patients from any cost: HHS must rebate what they pay or discount the drug at purchase so these patients face no economic burden from the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers would pay the excise tax on every milligram of active opioid they sell. Some of that cost could be passed through to retail prices; the bill's own reporting requirement acknowledges the risk, and while cancer and hospice patients are guaranteed rebates, other patients in pain would bear any passed-through cost unless prices did not rise. Because treatment funding comes only from net revenue after rebates, the funding stream also shrinks if opioid sales fall.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid makers; some patients via prices

drawbacks.text: The tax could raise retail prices, and the rebate guarantee covers only cancer and hospice patients — other people living with pain would absorb any passed-through cost. The bill itself requires an HHS study of the tax's impact on retail opioid prices and patient access, an acknowledgment that this risk was real.

The tax touches only legally manufactured prescription opioids, so it does nothing about the illicit heroin and fentanyl that were driving much of the epidemic's death toll, and raising the price of legal painkillers does not by itself keep pills from being diverted or misused.

Treatment funding would ride on sales volume: the money available to states is whatever net revenue the tax raises after rebates, so the funding stream is unpredictable and shrinks if opioid prescribing declines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the trade is a good one for ordinary people: a small per-milligram charge on manufacturers, with the heaviest users of opioids for legitimate medical need (cancer, hospice) and addiction-treatment drugs carved out, funds a treatment system that was badly underfunded during the epidemic. The honest caveats are that some non-exempt chronic pain patients could face higher prices, that the tax does nothing about illicit opioids, and that the treatment funding is only as reliable as opioid sales. These are design frictions, not fatal flaws.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees — Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce — and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, late in the second session of a Congress dominated by the opioid debate, and no other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The Speaker referred it to two committees with jurisdiction — Ways and Means for the tax, Energy and Commerce for the health programs — and neither took it up.
There were no further actions of any kind after the referral; the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers, who never paid the tax; no state ever received the dedicated treatment funding, and patients with addiction were left with whatever treatment money existed before the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid makers; no new treatment funding arrived

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republican or other member cosponsored it, and no vote was ever recorded, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Would have paid one cent per milligram on every opioid painkiller sold — a direct charge on the companies making and importing these drugs during the years their products fueled the epidemic. The bill's death means the tax was never collected.

The bill earmarked the tax revenue for building new residential and outpatient treatment facilities, sober living homes, and neonatal care, with higher reimbursement for providers in underserved communities. Providers lost a dedicated funding stream when the bill died.
